newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless claims jump dismissed as temporary.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless claims jump dismissed as temporary.

text.p: A recent jump in new U.S. jobless claims is due to temporary automobile retooling layoffs and most likely does not signal fresh weakness in the labor market, economists said Thursday.
The Labor Department reported that new jobless claims climbed sharply, to 377,000 in the week ended July 5 from 337,000 a week earlier.
The government said the rise was driven at least in part by anticipated shutdowns in the automobile industry as factories were retooled for new models.

"The Labor Department official took the sting out of the report," said Christopher Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi. "This year, the (auto) shutdowns were well advertised and the market isn't biting the idea that the labor market is weak."
Bond prices moved up from pre-report levels immediately after the jobless claims data were released, but they quickly moved down again.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 9/32 to 100-16/32, yielding 6.59 percent, a half hour after the jobless claims news came out.
Rupkey said the report had not changed investors' or economists' perception of the labor market.

"Most people assume that the labor market is in very, very good condition and that everyone who is willing and able to work can find work, so these data do not ring true with what we think we know to be the case," said Rupkey.

"The jobless claims data are to be ignored because of the auto plant shutdowns for retooling," said Josh Feinman, global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "Those always happen this time of year, but the exact timing and magnitude varies so it's difficult for the seasonal adjustments to cope with them."
Feiman said that in August, "when things settle back to normal," investors will get "the real reading on jobless claims."
Peter D'Antonio, senior economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A., agreed.

"The seasonals don't know in which week the auto plant shutdowns will occur so they can't adjust exactly and you get a lot of wild swings," he said. "You can get higher or lower numbers in July and in the first week of August, also, depending on when the retooling-related layoffs occur."
Still, economists noted that jobless claims crept higher in June.
The Labor Department said the four-week moving average for jobless claims stood at 339,000 for the four weeks ended June 28, up from 335,750 for the four weeks ended June 14.
"The labor market and the economy are not as strong as they were in the earliest months of the year, but they're by no means weak," said Feinman.

"In terms of what we've seen on a trend basis for claims, they have picked up quite a bit in the last several weeks from what I would call very, very low figures earlier in the year," said D'Antonio. "That pickup was associated with the rising unemployment rate."
The jobless rate rose to 5.0 percent in June from 4.8 percent in May.

"We had a pickup in claims in June that indicated that the labor market wasn't quite as strong as it was in the beginning of the year," said D'Antonio. "But as far as the jobless claims we learned about today, that's just temporary volatility."
